text: This study aims to evaluate the load response of various end-use devices to hourly dynamic prices. The end-uses studied here are space cooling, space heating, water heating, crop irrigation, pool and spa pumps, and electric vehicle (EV) charging, all for both residential and commercial applications, except for crop irrigation. By modeling possible price-responsive load dispatch algorithms and assessing the resulting impacts on both individual bills and the overall grid, we seek to inform policymakers and utilities about the potential benefits and challenges associated with dynamic pricing, and considerations for the design of dynamic pricing tariffs. Additionally, we will explore the cost-effectiveness of adopting automation technologies to enable devices to respond more effectively to real-time price signals. This study considers a range of price profiles, accounting for differences across utilities and customer classes, and presents scenarios for dynamic price design via variation in the percentage of total customer electric costs that are allocated dynamically (versus constituting a fixed portion of the hourly volumetric price). We present results focused primarily on 2030, forecasting electricity prices under both low and high-cost scenarios, to inform longer-term tariff design considerations. 1.1 California load flexibility research Since 2014, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) has performed multiple analyses on behalf of the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) which assess and forecast the potential flexible load resources that are available within the investor owned utility (IOU) service territories that the CPUC regulates. The CPUC Energy Division has funded this long-standing body of work to inform State demand response (DR) and other load-flexibility policy making efforts which seek to incorporate cost-effective and valuable load flexible resources into energy system planning and operations. The California Price Response Potential Study builds on the products of four earlier phases of the DR Potential Study, as well as a more recent suite of dynamic pricing studies, to understand and map the resources that load flexibility can provide to support State energy goals. Here we contextualize the current study in the context of previous phases of the LBNL-CPUC load 1 flexible resource research effort. Note that the analytic framework underlying this and previous studies groups DR services into four core categories: shape,1 shift,2 shed,3 and shimmy.4 Phase 1 Report: Alstone et al. (2016) summarized the shed DR resource, with a focus on supporting the immediate needs of stakeholders, policymakers, and intervenors in CPUC rulemaking R.013-09-011. This multi-year rulemaking was initiated to “Enhance the Role or DR in Meeting the State’s Resource Planning Needs and Operational Requirements.” The Phase 1 report documented that there is a large potential shed resource (ranging from 2-8 GW depending on assumptions about value and R&D pathway). It also demonstrated how our modeling approach to DR analysis could be used to weigh the benefits of flexibility and load control against other options like battery deployment and conventional generation resources. Phase 2 Report: Alstone et al. (2017) was the final report in support of R.013-09-011 and expanded the set of DR resources being considered to include shift, shape, and shimmy in addition to the shed resource.
